translationRepairs: After the Six Xiu disaster, most survivors fled south with Ren Ziyun, Liu Kun's designated heir.
After the Six Xiu disaster, most survivors fled south with Zun, Liu Kun's designated heir.
劉琨任子遵 is Liu Kun's heir-son Zun; Ren Ziyun fuses 任子 with 遵 into a false personal name and must be corrected.
Xiong styled himself Shiyuan and Dan Shiya; both were bold, resourceful men who had served as provincial aides under the Jin.
Xiong's style was Shiyuan, and Dan's was Shiya; both were bold, resourceful men who had served as provincial aides under the Jin.
雄字世遠，澹字世雅 assigns courtesy names separately; without a break after Shiyuan, “styled himself Shiyuan and Dan Shiya” makes both names Xiong's complement, so the clearer split attribution is required.
Then Xiong and Dan, with Ren Ziyun, Liu Kun's heir, led tens of thousands of Wuhuan and Jin followers into open revolt.
Then Xiong and Dan, with Zun, Liu Kun's heir, led tens of thousands of Wuhuan and Jin followers into open revolt.
與劉琨任子遵 again names heir-son Zun; Ren Ziyun is the same fused misreading as in s0107 and is not supported by the Chinese.
Fu Jian gave Liu Kuren's wife the surname Gongsun and loaded her with gifts.
Fu Jian bestowed a Gongsun woman on Liu Kuren as his wife and provided her with a rich dowry.
賜庫仁妻公孫氏 means Fu Jian bestowed a Gongsun-clan woman as Kuren's wife, confirmed by later 妻兄公孫希; giving an existing wife the surname Gongsun invents a rename the Chinese does not state.
"Outward campaigns also repelled": Northern History juan 20, this life, has dong (campaign) for xun (merit).
"Outward campaigns also repelled": Northern History juan 20, this life, has xun (merit) where this text has dong (campaign).
「動」作「勳」 reports that Beishi has 勳 where this text has 動; “has dong for xun” reverses that collation direction, and the proposed wording restores it.

Wei Cao set up a stele south of Dahang city. In Qian's Textual Notes, juan 38, we read: "This chapter preserves his inscription in full, yet the historiographers mangled the record and the authentic text was lost.

Wei Cao set up a stele south of Dahang city. In Qian's Textual Notes, juan 38, we read: "This biography records the stele Wei Cao erected; alas, the historiographers altered it and its original authenticity was lost.
此傳載衞操所立碑 only says the biography records the stele; “preserves…in full” invents completeness, and the proposed wording better tracks 惜為史臣改竄，失其本真.
